hints: Start by thinking about the word non-self. What does your immune system have to decide when it meets a molecule on a bacterium or virus?
Think about what type of large biological molecules are most variable and stick out on cell surfaces - what are pathogen surfaces mostly made of?
Link the antigen to what happens next - which cells recognise it and what specific protein is made to bind to it?
walkthrough:
What non-self really means**
Think of every cell in your body carrying a set of familiar ID tags. Anything with a different shape that your lymphocytes have never seen as self will trigger a response. So a non-self antigen is any molecule that stimulates an immune response because it is recognised as foreign.

What they are made of**
Most antigens are large, complex molecules with a unique 3D shape. They are usually proteins or glycoproteins, sometimes polysaccharides. That is why bacterial walls, flagella, viral capsids and protein coats are so antigenic - they present lots of foreign protein shapes on the outside.

How the body deals with them**
The key feature is specific recognition. Receptors on B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes, and antibodies released by plasma cells, have a complementary shape to one particular antigen. Binding activates phagocytes and lymphocytes and leads to production of that specific antibody, so you need to state both recognition and antibody production to get full credit.

Final answer: Stimulates an immune response. Usually a protein / glycoprotein / polysaccharide. Recognised by immune cells e.g. B- / T-lymphocytes / macrophages and causes production of specific antibodies that bind to it. Found on surface of pathogens / infected cells e.g. bacterial cell wall, viral capsid.

hints: Sort the four cells by job - which two are lymphocytes that can still divide, and which one is the end-stage antibody factory?
Remember who is the coordinator. Which T cell releases chemical messages to activate B cells, T-killer cells and phagocytes?
For the last row, think about first meeting with a virus - do you already have plasma cells and memory cells, or do all these cell types have to be made from scratch?
Check the plasma cell row carefully - if a cell is fully specialised for making antibody protein, can it still go through mitosis and can it make a different protein like cytokine?
walkthrough:
Who can do clonal expansion**
When a B-lymphocyte, T-helper cell or T-killer cell meets its specific antigen it is activated to divide by mitosis many times to make a clone. That is clonal expansion. Plasma cells are different - they are what B-lymphocytes differentiate into. They are terminally differentiated, packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum for antibody secretion, and do not divide further. So B, T-helper, T-killer tick, plasma cross.

Who secretes cytokine as its main role**
Cytokines are messenger proteins. The main cytokine secretor is the T-helper cell. It releases interleukins to stimulate B cells to divide and form plasma cells, stimulate T-killer cells, and activate phagocytes. B-lymphocytes make receptors and become antibody makers, plasma cells make antibodies, T-killer cells kill infected cells directly. So only T-helper ticks.

Who is present in a primary response**
Primary means first exposure to that virus. You still need the whole humoral and cell-mediated response to develop: specific B-lymphocytes are activated, some become plasma cells to make antibody, T-helper cells coordinate, T-killer cells destroy infected cells. All four types are produced and present, so the last row is all ticks.

Final answer: Row 1 clonal expansion: B-lymphocyte tick, plasma cell cross, T-helper cell tick, T-killer cell tick. Row 2 secrete cytokine: B-lymphocyte cross, plasma cell cross, T-helper cell tick, T-killer cell cross. Row 3 primary response to virus: all four tick.

hints: Picture mitosis finishing with two nuclei in one cell - what must happen next to split the cytoplasm into two separate cells?
Recall the two big phases of the cell cycle - mitosis (M) and the long growth phase between divisions. Which phase contains G1, S and G2?
The letter S gives a clue - what material must be exactly doubled before mitosis so each daughter gets a full set?
walkthrough:
A - What follows nuclear division**
Mitosis only divides the nucleus. Immediately after, the cytoplasm must divide to make two separate daughter cells. That is cytokinesis, usually by a cleavage furrow in animal cells. Do not confuse it with mitosis itself.

B - Where S phase lives**
The mitotic cell cycle is interphase plus mitosis plus cytokinesis. Interphase is the long part and is divided into G1, S and G2. So the S phase occurs inside interphase.

C - What S stands for**
S stands for synthesis. During S phase the main event is replication of DNA by semi-conservative replication. Each chromosome is copied to produce two identical sister chromatids, so DNA content doubles ready for mitosis.
Final answer: A = cytokinesis (division of cytoplasm). B = interphase. C = DNA replication / DNA synthesis to form sister chromatids.
